newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese veteran misses Deng funeral due to illness.
newsitem.headline: Chinese veteran misses Deng funeral due to illness.

text.p: The most senior of China's surviving revolutionaries after the death of Deng Xiaoping failed to attend memorial rites for his revolutionary comrade on Tuesday due to illness, Chinese sources said.
Peng Zhen, 95, one of Deng's closest associates and allies throughout a career that ended with his death, aged 92, last Wednesday, missed Deng's lying-in-state on Monday as well his memorial rites.
Peng was listed fourth on members of a 459-strong funeral committee headed by President Jiang Zemin formed last week for Deng. He was the most senior communist not to attend.

Peng was taken into the Beijing Hospital in the city centre, where the late Premier Zhou Enlai died of cancer in 1976, during the Chinese lunar new year festival, which fell on February 7 this year, the sources said.

Doctors hospitalised Peng, a former mayor of Beijing and head of the parliament, with severe vomiting and he was too weak to leave for final rites for Deng, said the sources, who declined to be identified.

His absence from the funeral was a signal that Peng may be seriously ill since China's five other most senior surviving revolutionary leaders all attended Deng's lying-in-state and memorial rites, although several appeared frail and weak.

They were former president Yang Shangkun, 89, ex-parliament chief Wan Li, 81, retired Politburo standing committee member Song Ping, 80, former vice premier Bo Yibo, 90, and retired general Song Renqiong, 92.
Peng is a veteran hardliner who stepped down from that post in April 1988 as part of a drive to retire aging communist comrades, but retained widespread influence.

Mayor of Beijing for 15 years and a close ally of then head of state Liu Shaoqi, Peng was hounded from office in June, 1966, by radicals charging he had transformed Beijing into a personal empire from which to combat Chairman Mao Zedong's policies.

He returned to prominence in the late 1970s along with longtime ally, Deng, and was appointed chairman of the National People's Congress in 1983, a job that afforded him ample opportunity to build a powerbase.
In 1979, Peng was named to head a legal commission set up by the parliament to help it to strengthen China's battered legal system and "guarantee the People's democracy".
